newsitem.title: FRANCE: Seguin bids to lead defeated French Gaullists.
newsitem.headline: Seguin bids to lead defeated French Gaullists.

text.p: Former National Assembly speaker Philippe Seguin put himself forward on Thursday to take over as leader of France's Gaullist RPR party from defeated prime minister Alain Juppe after the left swept to power.
"Mr Seguin...will submit his candidacy as president of the movement," a statement from his office said.

Seguin, a leader of the "no" campaign when French voters approved the Maastricht treaty on European union in a 1992 referendum, said he would also stand as interim parliamentary floor leader of the party founded by conservative President Jacques Chirac.
The parliamentary caucus elects its officers next Tuesday.

Juppe has been under pressure to resign as president of the Rally for the Republic Party in favour of Seguin after the disastrous loss in Sunday's National Assembly election to new Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin.
Seguin emerged in the final days of the snap election campaign as Chirac's favourite to succeed the unpopular Juppe as prime minister, had the right held power.
Juppe has said he will call an emergency party congress for September to elect a new leader but failed to spell out if he would be a candidate.
Acting RPR secretary-general Jean-Louis Debre said on Thursday that he hoped the congress could be brought forward to July to end the bitter feuding.

"I'm among those who believe that, after a defeat, we must reflect, change structures, probably change leaders, but not any old way. We must do it responsibly, calmly, and with thought," Debre, outgoing interior minister, told Radio Monte Carlo.
"I would like the congress to take place in July," he said.

Francois Baroin, a Chirac speech writer and political adviser, said that it was "probably a good idea" to bring forward the congress to July. "It would solve the personality problems," he told France 2 television.

He rebuffed suggestions that Chirac was to blame for the crisis by calling the snap elections, wrongly calculating that he could win re-election for his centre-right allies until the end of his own seven-year presidential term in 2002.
"I believe that the overwhelming majority (of RPR members) have an unshakeable loyalty to Jacques Chirac and do not want the death of the RPR," he said.
